meta.title: The potential adverse effects of hypodermic glucagon-like peptide -1 receptor agonist on patients with type 2 diabetes: A population-based study.
meta.abstract:
Background

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a class of injectable antidiabetic drugs, have shown significant efficacies in improving glycemic and weight control in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the long-term safety of GLP-1 RAs remains insufficiently studied. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence on potential adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use in T2D patients without major chronic diseases including impaired cardiac or renal function.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 7746 T2D patients on GLP-1 RAs in Shenzhen, China. They were compared with 124 371 metformin-only users and 36 146 insulin-only users, forming two therapy control groups. GLP-1 RAs users were also further 1:2 paired with the control groups. Competing risk survival analyses were conducted to assess the incidence risks, presenting subdistributional hazard ratios (sHRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for various adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use.

Results

Compared with metformin-only users, GLP-1 RAs use was associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes (sHRs with 95% CIs), including pancreatitis (2.01, 1.24-3.24), acute nephritis (3.20, 2.17-4.70), kidney failure (3.73, 2.74-5.08), thyroid cancer (2.25, 1.23-4.10), and thyroid dysfunction (1.27, 1.00-1.63), respectively; Similar results were also found when compared with insulin-only users. Importantly, long-term (≥12 months) GLP-1 RAs use may further elevate the incidence risks of pancreatitis, acute nephritis, thyroid cancer, and thyroid dysfunction.

Conclusion

Compared with traditional T2D treatments, GLP-1 RAs use may be associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes in a Chinese population. Cautions were strongly warranted in the use of GLP-1 RAs. Further validation is crucial across diverse populations.

domains.name: Confounding
domains.direction_justification: GLP-1 RA users had significantly higher baseline socioeconomic status (75.60% citizen health insurance vs 54.96% in metformin; 26.07% undergraduate education vs 11.94% in metformin) and higher obesity rates (13.21% BMI 30-39.9 vs 4.87% in metformin, Table 3S). Critical clinical confounders were heavily missing (HbA1c was missing in 91.27% and FPG in 33.22% across matched cohorts, Table 1), and 'unspecified' was matched as an explicit covariate category (e.g., unspecified BMI was 32.49% vs 32.71% in GLP-1 RA vs metformin). Uncontrolled baseline disease severity and health-seeking behavior drive hazard ratios away from the null.

domains.name: Selection of participants into the study
domains.direction_justification: Defining treatment cohorts by cumulative medication usage across the entire follow-up period ('lasting from baseline date to last follow-up date with other diabetic prescriptions <6 months') conditions cohort eligibility on post-baseline survival and adherence, introducing immortal time bias and selection bias that artificially concentrates events among continuous users.

findings.title: Post-baseline exposure conditioning and massive exclusions
findings.mechanism: Cohorts were defined based on cumulative medication use throughout the entire follow-up rather than at baseline (new-user design), introducing immortal time bias and selection bias.
evidence: Out of 985,278 initial diabetes patients, 362,035 were excluded for missing prescription data and 177,381 for missing IDs (Figure 1)
GLP-1 RA group was defined as patients whose prescription lasted from baseline to last follow-up with other medications <6 months (Methods 2.1)

domains.name: Post-exposure interventions
domains.direction_justification: Discontinuation due to acute side effects was modeled as a competing risk rather than an adverse event of the drug strategy, altering the risk set dynamically across groups.

findings.title: Acute side effects classified as competing risks rather than outcomes
findings.mechanism: Discontinuation from acute symptoms (diarrhea, emesis, dizziness, arrhythmia) was treated as a competing risk in subdistribution hazard models, potentially censoring or modifying the effective follow-up duration differentially across drug classes.
evidence: Competing events systematically defined by acute symptoms including diarrhea/emesis, dermatitis tetter, acne, dizziness, arrhythmia (Methods 2.3)
Mean follow-up was 23.7 months for GLP-1 RAs, 23.2 months for insulin, and 24.8 months for metformin (Methods 2.2)

domains.name: Missing data
domains.direction_justification: Over 90% of patients lacked HbA1c values (GLP-1 RAs: 90.52%, insulin: 91.79%, metformin: 90.45%), over 30% lacked FPG values, and over 32% lacked BMI values. Treating missing values as an 'unspecified' category in PSM matches individuals on the presence of missing data rather than on actual clinical similarity.

findings.title: Critical laboratory and biometric data missing in vast majority of cohort
findings.mechanism: Propensity score matching included 'unspecified' as a category for age, education, marital status, and BMI, while HbA1c was completely omitted from matching due to >90% missingness.
evidence: HbA1c missingness was 91.27% in the PSM population (Table 1)
Fasting plasma glucose missingness was 33.22% in the PSM population (Table 1)
BMI was unspecified in 33.81% of GLP-1 RA users and 36.08% of insulin users (Table 1)
Education was unspecified in 33.62% of GLP-1 RA users and 35.89% of insulin users (Table 1)

domains.name: Measurement of the outcome
domains.direction_justification: GLP-1 RA patients had higher insurance coverage (75.6% vs 55.0% in metformin, Table 3S) and regular clinic visits for injectable therapies, increasing diagnostic surveillance and opportunistic detection of incidental conditions like thyroid cancer (sHR: 2.25, 95% CI: 1.23-4.10), thyroid dysfunction (sHR: 1.27, 95% CI: 1.00-1.63), and renal failure (sHR: 3.73, 95% CI: 2.74-5.08).

findings.title: Surveillance and diagnostic workup bias via ICD-10 text mining
findings.mechanism: Outcomes were identified via ICD-10 codes and regular expression keyword matching in EMR records without blinded adjudication. Patients on newly initiated, closely monitored injectable drugs are subject to greater diagnostic scrutiny and routine biochemical monitoring.
evidence: Outcomes identified via ICD-10 and regular expression terminology match across outpatient and hospitalization records (Table 2S)
Elevated risks observed across unrelated organs including skin follicular cysts (sHR: 2.03, 95% CI: 1.24-3.30 vs insulin) and leukemia (sHR: 15.09, 95% CI: 4.65-48.98 vs metformin, Figure 3)

domains.name: Selection of the reported result
domains.direction_justification: Testing dozens of ICD-10 outcome categories across multiple subgroups (4 specific agents, 2 duration strata, 2 distinct control groups) without pre-registration or multiple-comparison adjustment produces extreme, statistically fragile effect estimates (e.g., leukemia sHR: 15.09, 95% CI: 4.65-48.98).

findings.title: Multiple hypothesis testing and selective highlighting of extreme hazard ratios
findings.mechanism: Evaluating over 18 distinct adverse disease categories across 4 drug agents, 2 duration cutoffs, and 2 comparator groups generates substantial multiplicity, with selective narrative focus on extreme associations.
evidence: 18 distinct disease categories evaluated across digestive, renal, thyroid, skin, and lymphatic/hematopoietic systems (Table 2S)
Leukemia sHR reported as 15.09 (95% CI: 4.65-48.98) after >=12 months GLP-1 RA use vs metformin (Figure 3)
Subgroup analyses split across 4 GLP-1 RA agents with varying sample sizes down to N=267 for loxenatide (Table 5S)

overall.summary: This retrospective observational study exhibits a very high risk of bias across multiple ROBINS-E domains. Major methodological flaws include defining treatment groups based on cumulative post-baseline adherence (introducing selection and immortal time bias), extreme missingness in primary clinical confounders (HbA1c missing in >90% of participants, BMI missing in >32%), treating 'unspecified' missing categories as matched strata in propensity score matching, unadjudicated electronic health record outcome identification susceptible to diagnostic surveillance bias, and unadjusted multiple testing yielding implausible effect sizes (e.g., sHR 15.09 for leukemia). These biases consistently push effect estimates away from the null.

baseline_comparability.summary: GLP-1 RA users were markedly more obese (BMI 30-39.9: 13.21% vs 4.87% in metformin) and had substantially higher health insurance coverage and educational attainment at baseline than controls. time_related_biases.summary: The study uses a predominant-user design that classifies baseline exposure using full follow-up treatment history, introducing immortal time and selection biases. In addition, assessing cancer and chronic outcomes with no lag period over a mean follow-up of only 23.7 months creates severe protopathic and detection biases that artificially inflate apparent drug harms.
